section: Case Study — Haramain High Speed Railway: WBS Coordination Across Borders
text:
Case Study — Haramain High Speed Railway: WBS Coordination Across Borders






Important🏭 Case Study: Haramain High Speed Railway — When Integration Fails at Scale



Background:
The Haramain High Speed Railway (قطار الحرمين السريع — HHR) connects the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah via Jeddah and King Abdullah Economic City, spanning 450 kilometres at speeds up to 300 km/h. This is the Arab world’s flagship rail project, operating in one of the most challenging environments on Earth — the Hejaz Mountains and the Arabian Desert.
Original Plan vs Actual: - Contract signed: 2009 - Original completion: 2013 - Actual opening: October 2018 (5 years late) - Budget: ~$16.5 billion (USD)
The WBS Problem:
The programme was divided between four major international consortia, each operating under different engineering standards and document management systems:








Consortium
Nationality
Scope




Al Shoula Group / Saudi Binladin Group
Saudi
Civil works — earthworks, structures, track foundation


Al Rajhi / China Railway Engineering
Chinese-Saudi
Northern civil works alignment


RENFE / CAF / Ineco
Spanish
Railway systems, signalling, rolling stock, operations


Siemens / Alstom
European
Electrification and E&M systems



Each consortium applied its own CAD standards, document numbering systems, and interface protocols — with no unified digital coordination environment across the programme.
What Happened:
- Civil works were substantially complete by 2013, but systems integration — connecting trains, signalling, electrification, and station systems — caused a further 5 years of delays - The interface between European-standard rail systems and Saudi civil infrastructure was managed informally, with no dedicated interface register - In 2016, a crisis at Saudi Binladin Group (the Kingdom’s largest contractor, suspended following safety incidents) forced urgent contractor replacement across 300+ km of residual civil works - Testing and commissioning of 40 stations required re-coordination of 12 separate sub-systems, each owned by a different consortium
Impact:







Factor
Effect




5-year programme delay
Billions in financing and standing costs


Contractor suspension (SBG)
6+ months for retendering and remobilisation


Signalling integration failures
18 additional months of testing and rectification


Interface ambiguity
300+ formal interface non-conformances logged



Project Management Root Causes:








Failure
Root Cause
PM Lesson




No unified interface register
Each consortium managed its own interfaces
Create a Programme Interface Register owned by an independent systems integrator


Four different CAD/document standards
No standardisation mandated at contract award
Mandate a single BIM/document management platform at programme initiation


Late commissioning focus
Testing planned as a single terminal activity
Overlap testing with construction using rolling section commissioning


Contractor financial collapse
No annual contractor capability re-assessment
Include contractor financial health reviews as a governance requirement in mega-contracts



The Achievement:
Despite its troubled delivery, the HHR now carries hundreds of thousands of pilgrims between Makkah and Madinah annually, reducing the historic 4–6 hour road journey to 2.5 hours by train — the Arab world’s first true high-speed railway.
Discussion Questions: 1. How should the WBS dictionary have addressed the interface between civil works (SBG scope) and railway systems (RENFE scope)? 2. What governance structure would you design to manage a four-consortium programme of this scale? 3. How does this case compare to the Airbus A380 integration failure? What structural similarities exist?
Sources: Saudi Railways Organisation (2018); Arab Union of Railways (2017)

Caution✏️ Exercise 3.1 — Requirements Collection



You are PM for the design and construction of a new university engineering laboratory (1,500 m²).

Identify at least 8 categories of stakeholders who would have requirements for this lab

Caution✏️ Exercise 3.2 — Build a WBS



For the construction of a new community footbridge (80m span, steel throughtruss, timber deck, two abutments), develop a complete WBS that:

Has at least 4 levels of decomposition
Includes ALL project phases (from charter to closure)
Contains at least 30 work packages at level 4

Includes a WBS Dictionary entry for 5 of the work packages

Caution✏️ Exercise 3.3 — Scope Statement Writing



A client has given you the following brief:

“We want you to fix our factory’s compressed air system. The compressors keep breaking down and it’s costing us $80,000 a year in repairs and lost production.”

Write a Scope Statement for this project that includes: 1. Project scope description 2. List of deliverables (minimum 6) 3. Acceptance criteria for at least 3 deliverables 4. Explicit exclusions (minimum 4 things that are NOT in scope) 5. Key assumptions (minimum 3) 6. Key constraints (minimum 2)








Caution✏️ Exercise 3.4 — Change Control Scenario



You are PM of a $3.5M road reconstruction project (12 months). You are in Month 4.
The client project manager calls you and says: > “We’ve had a great idea. While you’ve got the road dug up, can you install a new stormwater pipe underneath? The council surveyed it last week and it will need replacing in 3 years anyway. Saves us digging it up twice.”

Is this a reasonable request? Argue both for and against
Prepare an Impact Assessment covering: scope, schedule, cost, risk, and quality
What additional information would you need before completing the assessment?
Draft a Change Request Form (use the fields: ID, Date, Description, Requestor, Impact Summary, PM Recommendation)
How would you respond to the client verbally while the formal assessment is in progress?

title: 7  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
7.2 Activity Definition and Duration Estimating

7.2.1 From Work Packages to Activities
Work packages from the WBS must be further broken down into schedule activities — the individual tasks that can be tracked on a daily/weekly basis.







WBS Work Package
Schedule Activities




1.3.1 Foundation Design
A1: Geotechnical data review; A2: Foundation type analysis; A3: Structural calculations; A4: Foundation drawings; A5: Specification writing


1.4.2 Concrete Structures
B1: Formwork fabrication; B2: Reinforcement fixing; B3: Concrete pouring; B4: Curing; B5: Formwork striking; B6: Surface finishing





7.2.2 Duration Estimation Methods

Analogous EstimatingParametric EstimatingThree-Point (PERT) EstimatingBottom-Up Estimating


Use historical data from similar projects

Fast and low effort
Less accurate
Best for early-stage estimates

Example: “Our last 50MW substation took 18 months, so this 60MW substation will take about 21 months”
Accuracy: ±25% to ±50%


Use statistical relationships between variables

Uses unit rates or formulas
More accurate than analogous
Requires reliable data

Example: “Excavation rate for this soil type is 120m³/day with a 20-tonne excavator. We have 2,400m³ to excavate, so: 2,400 ÷ 120 = 20 days”
Accuracy: ±10% to ±25%


Use optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates
Three estimates for each activity: - Optimistic (O): Best case, everything goes right - Most Likely (M): Most realistic estimate - Pessimistic (P): Worst case, everything goes wrong
PERT Expected Duration: \[t_E = \frac{O + 4M + P}{6}\]
PERT Standard Deviation: \[\sigma = \frac{P - O}{6}\]
PERT Variance: \[\sigma^2 = \left(\frac{P - O}{6}\right)^2\]


Estimate each activity individually, then aggregate

Most accurate method
Most time-consuming
Best for detailed planning

Process: 1. Identify all activities 2. Estimate each individually with subject matter experts 3. Sum all activities for total project duration 4. Add buffer/contingency
Accuracy: ±5% to ±15%

title: 7  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
7.3 Activity Sequencing — Dependency Types
Activities must be sequenced based on their logical dependencies:


  
  
    
      Finish-to-Start (FS)
      Most Common
    
    
      Activity A
      ⟶
      Activity B
    
    B cannot start until A finishes
    e.g. Excavation must finish before concrete pour starts
  

  
  
    Start-to-Start (SS)
    
      Activity A
      ⟶
      Activity B
    
    B cannot start until A starts
    e.g. Training can begin once documentation starts
  

  
  
    Finish-to-Finish (FF)
    
      Activity A
      ⟶
      Activity B
    
    B cannot finish until A finishes
    e.g. QA testing cannot end until development ends
  

  
  
    
      Start-to-Finish (SF)
      Rare
    
    
      Activity A
      ⟶
      Activity B
    
    B cannot finish until A starts
    e.g. New system (A) starts → old system (B) can shut down
  



7.3.1 Lag and Lead Time

Lag: A delay after a dependency is satisfied

Example: Concrete curing — next activity starts 7 days after pouring finishes (FS + 7 days lag)

Lead: An overlap — the successor activity starts before the predecessor finishes

Example: Begin procurement drawings while detailed design is still 80% complete (FS - 2 weeks lead)

title: 7  Project Scheduling & Critical Path Method
text:
7.5 Critical Path Method (CPM)
The Critical Path Method (CPM) identifies the longest path through the network — the sequence of activities that determines the minimum project duration.






Note📖 CPM Basic Terms & Formulas











Term
Formula
Meaning




ES — Early Start
\(ES = \max(EF \text{ of predecessors})\)
Earliest an activity can start


EF — Early Finish
\(EF = ES + Duration\)
Earliest an activity can finish


LF — Late Finish
\(LF = \min(LS \text{ of successors})\)
Latest it can finish without delaying the project


LS — Late Start
\(LS = LF - Duration\)
Latest it can start without delaying the project


Total Float
\(Float = LS - ES \;=\; LF - EF\)
Flexibility an activity has before it delays the project


Free Float
\(FF = ES_{successor} - EF\)
Flexibility before delaying the next activity


Critical Path
Activities where \(Float = 0\)
Longest path — determines total project duration


Critical Activity
\(Float = 0\)
Any delay on this activity delays the entire project






7.5.1 Step-by-Step CPM Calculation

Step 1: Forward Pass (Calculate ES and EF)






Tip💡 Starting Convention



The first activity always has ES = 0 by convention — the project clock starts at zero. The formula \(ES = \max(EF \text{ of predecessors})\) only applies to activities that have predecessors. Similarly, in the backward pass, LF of the last activity = project duration (not calculated from successors).


\[ES_A = 0 \quad \text{(by convention — no predecessors)}, \quad EF_A = ES_A + Duration_A = 0 + 3 = 3\]
\[ES_B = EF_A = 3, \quad EF_B = 3 + 5 = 8\]
\[ES_C = EF_A = 3, \quad EF_C = 3 + 4 = 7\]
\[ES_D = EF_B = 8, \quad EF_D = 8 + 6 = 14\]
\[ES_E = \max(EF_B, EF_C) = \max(8, 7) = 8, \quad EF_E = 8 + 3 = 11\]
\[ES_F = \max(EF_D, EF_E) = \max(14, 11) = 14, \quad EF_F = 14 + 4 = 18\]
Project Duration = 18 days
Step 2: Backward Pass (Calculate LS and LF)
\[LF_F = 18 \quad \text{(by convention — equals project duration, no successors)}, \quad LS_F = LF_F - Duration_F = 18 - 4 = 14\]
\[LF_D = LS_F = 14, \quad LS_D = 14 - 6 = 8\]
\[LF_E = LS_F = 14, \quad LS_E = 14 - 3 = 11\]
\[LF_B = \min(LS_D, LS_E) = \min(8, 11) = 8, \quad LS_B = 8 - 5 = 3\]
\[LF_C = LS_E = 11, \quad LS_C = 11 - 4 = 7\]
\[LF_A = \min(LS_B, LS_C) = \min(3, 7) = 3, \quad LS_A = 3 - 3 = 0\]
Step 3: Calculate Float
\[Total\ Float = LS - ES = LF - EF\]

7.6.1 Gantt Chart Best Practices

What to IncludeMilestonesBaseline vs. Current



All Level 3-4 WBS activities
Milestones at key decision points
Critical path activities (highlighted in red or marked as critical)
Dependencies shown as arrows (where tools allow)
Resource allocations (who is responsible for each bar)
Planned vs. Actual tracking capability
Baseline vs. Current schedule view



Milestones are zero-duration events marking significant project achievements:
Common engineering project milestones: - ✓ Project Kick-off - ✓ Investigations Complete - ✓ 30% Design Issue for Review - ✓ 60% Design Issue for Review - ✓ 100% Design Issue for Construction - ✓ Regulatory Approval Received - ✓ Construction Start - ✓ Structural Works Complete - ✓ Commissioning Complete - ✓ Practical Completion - ✓ Defects Liability Period End


A well-managed Gantt chart always shows:

Baseline (original approved schedule) — shown as the lower bar or grey shadow
Current (updated actual progress) — shown as the main coloured bar
% Complete — progress indicator on each bar

If Current = Baseline, the project is on track.
If Current extends beyond Baseline, analysis is needed.

7.7 PERT Analysis — Handling Schedule Uncertainty
PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique) extends CPM by acknowledging that activity durations are uncertain and modelling them probabilistically.

Project Expected Duration = Sum of expected durations on critical path
Project Standard Deviation: \[\sigma_{project} = \sqrt{\sum \sigma^2_{critical\ activities}}\]


7.7.2 Probability of Completion by Target Date
Using the normal distribution:
\[Z = \frac{T_{target} - T_{expected}}{\sigma_{project}}\]
Where \(T_{target}\) is the desired completion date and \(T_{expected}\) is the calculated expected completion.






Note📖 Example PERT Probability Calculation



Critical path expected duration: 65 days
Project standard deviation: 8.5 days
Client deadline: 75 days
\[Z = \frac{75 - 65}{8.5} = 1.18\]
From Z-table: P(Z ≤ 1.18) ≈ 88%
There is an 88% probability of completing the project within 75 days.
To achieve 95% probability: Need Z = 1.645 → \(T = 65 + (1.645 × 8.5) = 79\) days

When the calculated schedule exceeds the target date, two primary compression techniques are available:

7.8.1 Cost-Slope for Crashing
The cost-slope tells you how much it costs to shorten an activity by one unit of time:
\[Cost\ Slope = \frac{Crash\ Cost - Normal\ Cost}{Normal\ Duration - Crash\ Duration}\]
Crashing priority: Always crash the critical path activity with the lowest cost-slope first, then re-analyse.

section: Case Study — Qatar FIFA World Cup 2022: Scheduling the Unschedulable
text:
Case Study — Qatar FIFA World Cup 2022: Scheduling the Unschedulable






Important🏭 Case Study: Qatar 2022 — When the Deadline Cannot Move



Background:
On 21 November 2022, the FIFA World Cup opened at Al-Bayt Stadium in Al-Khor, Qatar — the first World Cup hosted by an Arab nation. For Qatar’s Supreme Committee for Delivery & Legacy (SC), the scheduling challenge was unique: the tournament date was set in December 2010 and could not shift by even a single day. This created a project scheduling environment where float on the critical path was, ultimately, zero.
The Scale: - 8 world-class stadiums built or substantially reconstructed (most World Cup hosts refurbish existing facilities) - Hard deadline: 21 November 2022 — fixed 12 years in advance - Construction workforce: 30,000+ workers across stadium sites simultaneously - Largest stadium: Lusail Stadium (88,966 capacity) — the centrepiece venue for the final
Scheduling Challenges:







Challenge
Response




Summer temperatures reaching 50°C made daytime work impossible June–September
Shifted all critical construction to mandatory night shifts (22:00–06:00); stadium cooling systems tested 18 months early to enable summer commissioning


COVID-19 pandemic (March 2020) halted construction for 4–6 weeks
Critical path reassessed immediately; non-critical works suspended; critical path workers resumed in isolated bubbles within 3 weeks


Lusail Stadium — largest design, started last
Assigned highest resource density of any stadium; 24-hour operations from 2018; Lusail became first stadium to complete trial events in 2021 despite being the last to start


Al-Thumama Stadium required partial structural redesign mid-construction
Design frozen at 60% completion; structural changes fast-tracked through review cycles; construction sequence reordered around the redesigned elements


All 8 stadiums required fully operational cooling systems before commissioning began
MEP commissioning placed on the critical path from contract start — 3 months bought back by accelerating installation sequence



CPM Application:
The SC’s scheduling team used Oracle Primavera P6 Enterprise with a master programme of 35,000+ activities. The critical path ran through Lusail Stadium’s seating bowl and roof structure — the most complex and the last to mobilise. Any activity reaching < 5 days of total float triggered an automatic Managing Director-level review within 24 hours.
The Fixed Deadline Strategy: 1. Each stadium committed to completion 6 months before the tournament — allowing full test event cycles 2. Three rounds of test events per stadium: Fan Experience Tests, Operational Readiness Tests, and FIFA Final Certification 3. A parallel maximum acceleration schedule was pre-approved and ready to activate — with pre-agreed resource profiles and contractor incentive payments — if the primary programme was ever threatened
Outcome:
All 8 stadiums were delivered on or before their committed test event dates. The tournament opened on its announced date. Qatar Stadium 974 — a temporary venue built from shipping containers — was delivered as a surprise late addition and met its commissioning deadline.
Key Scheduling Lessons: 1. When the deadline is absolute, schedule contingency must be proportionally large — planning to finish “just in time” is planning to fail 2. External disruptions (COVID, extreme heat) will invalidate sections of any schedule — the organisations that survived maintained pre-developed recovery plans 3. Risk-driven sequencing: the most complex activities (Lusail’s roof) were started earliest and given the most resources 4. Automatic escalation triggers on critical float are more reliable than human judgment — at 5 days of float with 30,000 workers in play, human review is too slow
Sources: Supreme Committee for Delivery & Legacy (2022); Supreme Committee for Delivery & Legacy (2023)

8.4 Resource Histograms and Levelling
A resource histogram shows the planned usage of a resource over time, making over-allocation visible:





xychart-beta
    title "Civil Engineer Allocation (Before Levelling)"
    x-axis ["Wk 1", "Wk 2", "Wk 3", "Wk 4", "Wk 5", "Wk 6", "Wk 7", "Wk 8"]
    y-axis "Hours/Week" 0 --> 70
    bar [40, 55, 70, 65, 45, 30, 25, 40]
    line [40, 40, 40, 40, 40, 40, 40, 40]


 Concept of resource histogram and levelling 



The line represents the maximum available hours (40 hrs/week). Bars above the line = over-allocation.

8.4.1 Resource Levelling vs. Resource Smoothing

Resource LevellingResource SmoothingStrategies for Constrained Resources


Adjust the schedule to eliminate over-allocation

Can extend the project end date to resolve peaks
Activities are delayed into their float periods
Used when resource constraints are absolute (only 1 specialist available)
The project end date may slip

Example: If a structural engineer is needed 60 hrs/week for 2 weeks, but is only available 40 hrs/week, delay one set of activities by 2 weeks.


Smooth usage without changing the end date

Uses float to shift activities without extending the project
Cannot extend the project end date
Only non-critical activities can be moved
May leave some over-allocation if float is insufficient

Example: Move a non-critical design task from Week 3 to Week 5 to reduce the engineer’s peak load.


When you cannot add more resource:

Overtime — extend working hours (expensive, unsustainable)
Subcontract — outsource some activities
Reduce scope — remove lower-priority deliverables
Extend timeline — negotiate deadline relief with client
Cross-training — train team members to cover skill gaps
Shift scheduling — two shifts on critical path activities
Prioritise — focus the constrained resource on critical path only

8.5 Team Development — Tuckman’s Model
The most widely used model of team development, Tuckman’s Forming-Storming-Norming-Performing model:

Warning⚠️ Common Mistake — Assuming Teams Start at “Performing”



One of the most common errors engineering PMs make is treating a newly assembled project team as if they are already high-performing. Even experienced professionals need time to develop working relationships, establish communication norms, and build trust.
Allow time in your schedule for team development. Teams that rush through Forming and Storming often cycle back through them at critical moments in the project.

title: 8  Resource Management
section: Case Study — Grand Egyptian Museum: Resource Management at Civilisational Scale
text:
Case Study — Grand Egyptian Museum: Resource Management at Civilisational Scale






Important🏭 Case Study: Grand Egyptian Museum, Cairo — Managing the World’s Largest Archaeological Museum



Background:
The Grand Egyptian Museum (المتحف المصري الكبير — GEM) near the Pyramids of Giza is the world’s largest archaeological museum, housing over 100,000 artefacts including the complete treasures of Tutankhamun’s tomb — displayed together for the first time. GEM is the most complex cultural construction project in the modern Arab world, requiring resource management across archaeological conservation, specialist construction, and international professional services simultaneously.
Scale: - Floor area: 93,000 m² - Construction cost: ~$1 billion (USD) - Construction started: 2002; Tutankhamun galleries opened: 2022 - Peak construction workforce: 12,000 workers on site simultaneously
Resource Management Challenges:
Labour Resources: - Specialist skills required: Conservation scientists, museum lighting engineers, acoustic designers, Egyptological curators — none available locally in sufficient numbers - Solution: International specialists hired on rotating 6-month contracts; partnership with Cairo University to provide 200+ trained conservators; national training programme created 800 Egyptian museum technicians who did not previously exist
Specialist Conservation Resource (The Parallel Programme): - The Tutankhamun galleries alone required 10 years of artefact conservation — a programme running parallel to construction - 5,000+ individual objects each required cataloguing, condition assessment, treatment, and custom display mount fabrication - Resource conflict: The same conservation scientists were needed by both the Tutankhamun programme and 90 other exhibition halls simultaneously - Solution: Conservation resource schedule maintained separately from construction programme with a dedicated 800m² on-site conservation laboratory
Equipment and Procurement Resources: - Main atrium roof: 24,000 m² of translucent alabaster panels — unique material requiring custom Italian fabrication equipment; 18-month delivery cycle - Atrium steel structure (5,000+ tonnes) required specialist cranes continuously in demand across 4 simultaneous erection zones - 300+ custom museum display cases designed and fabricated in Germany, Austria, and Italy — long-lead procurement that could not be accelerated
Multi-Cultural Team Integration: - Owner: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities - Construction Manager: Nippon Koei (Japan) + EHAF (Egypt)
- Main contractor: KRCC (Egyptian) with specialist packages from Italy, Japan, and Germany - Languages: Arabic, English, Japanese — creating documentation and communication challenges - PM Response: Trilingual coordination protocols; unified electronic document management; joint weekly progress meetings with all parties
Schedule Pressure from External Events: - The 2011 Egyptian Revolution and 2013 political transition caused 3 years of project suspension - Resource dispersal during suspension meant re-mobilisation phases lost key specialist personnel who had moved to other projects - Recovery required six months of intensive recruitment before construction could resume at full capacity
Outcome: The Tutankhamun galleries and Grand Hall opened in 2022 to international acclaim. Egypt’s heritage sector now has 800 trained museum technicians, a world-class conservation laboratory, and an institutional knowledge base that will support Egyptian museums for decades.
Key Resource Lessons: 1. Specialist resources for rare projects must be identified and secured years before they are needed — conservation scientists cannot be trained in 6 months 2. Multi-cultural teams with fundamentally different working standards require active management — language and documentation protocols must be agreed before work starts, not after problems emerge 3. Long-lead procurement must be on the critical path from day one — the alabaster panels nearly caused an 18-month delay 4. Political risk disperses resources faster than any technical problem — having a formal re-mobilisation plan is as important as the original resource plan
Sources: Grand Egyptian Museum Organisation (2022); Nippon Koei Co., Ltd. (2019)

9.1 Why Use MS Project?
Manual scheduling (spreadsheets, sticky notes, hand-drawn Gantt charts) becomes unmanageable once a project has more than 20–30 activities and multiple resources. Microsoft Project 2021 / Microsoft Project for Microsoft 365 automates:

Critical path calculation (updated instantly when you change a duration)

Professional reporting

Leave at 500 (used for resource levelling)



Click Statistics button at any time to see summary: start, finish, duration, work, cost.


9.4.3 Step 3 — Create a Custom Calendar
Project tab → Change Working Time → Create New Calendar

Name it (e.g., “Palestine Standard”)
Set working days: Sunday to Thursday, 08:00–17:00 (with 1-hour lunch break)
Set Friday and Saturday as non-working days
Add exceptions (public holidays):

Select the date on the calendar
Click Exceptions tab → enter name → set as non-working




9.4.4 Step 4 — Set Up the WBS / Summary Tasks
In the Gantt Chart view, enter your WBS phases as Summary Tasks:

Type the Phase 1 name (e.g., Initiation) in the Task Name column → press Enter
Type sub-tasks below it
Select the sub-tasks → Task tab → Indent Task (or press Alt+Shift+Right arrow)
The parent row becomes a summary task (bold, with a collapse arrow)







Tip



Keyboard shortcut: Alt+Shift+→ to indent (make child), Alt+Shift+← to outdent (make parent)


Structure your task list to mirror the WBS numbering:
1. Project: Smart Campus Wi-Fi Upgrade          ← Project Summary (auto)
   1. Initiation                                 ← Summary Task
      1.1 Develop Project Charter
      1.2 Stakeholder Register
      1.3 Kick-off Meeting                       ← Milestone
   2. Planning                                   ← Summary Task
      2.1 Network Site Survey
      2.2 Equipment Specification
      ...


9.4.5 Step 5 — Enter Durations
Click the Duration column next to each task and type: - 5d = 5 days - 3w = 3 weeks - 0d = milestone (diamond on Gantt) - 1w 2d = 1 week + 2 days = 7 days






Important



Task Mode: Check the Task Mode column. Set to Manually Scheduled only for tasks with fixed dates (e.g., contractual milestones). All other tasks should be Auto Scheduled so MS Project recalculates the schedule automatically when dependencies change.




9.4.6 Step 6 — Set Dependencies (Predecessors)
In the Predecessors column, type the row number of the predecessor task:







To create this
Type in Predecessors column




Finish-to-Start (default)
3 (task 3 must finish before this starts)


Finish-to-Start + 2 day lag
3FS+2d


Start-to-Start
3SS


Finish-to-Finish
3FF


Start-to-Start + 1 week lag
3SS+1w


Multiple predecessors
3,5,7



Alternatively, in Gantt Chart view, drag from the end of one task bar to the start of another to create a FS dependency.






Warning



Critical Path Check: After entering all dependencies, go to View → Gantt Chart and check Format → Critical Tasks (check the box). All critical path tasks will turn red. If your entire project is red, you likely have no dependencies set.




9.4.7 Step 7 — Enter Resources
Switch to Resource Sheet view (View tab → Resource Sheet):
Fill in one row per resource:



Column
Guidance




Resource Name
Full name or role (e.g., “Network Engineer”)


Type
Work / Material / Cost


Material Label
(for materials only, e.g., “m²”, “units”)


Initials
Auto-filled; can customise


Group
Department or team (e.g., “IT”, “Civil”)


Max. Units
100% = full time; 50% = part time


Std. Rate
e.g., ₪120/h


Ovt. Rate
e.g., ₪180/h


Cost/Use
Fixed cost each time resource is used


Accrue At
Start / End / Prorated (how cost is recorded)


Base Calendar
Which working calendar applies to this person





9.4.8 Step 8 — Assign Resources to Tasks
Switch back to Gantt Chart view. For each task:

Double-click the task → Task Information dialog → Resources tab
Select the resource name from the dropdown
Set Units (e.g., 100% for full time on this task, 50% for half time)
Click OK

Or use the Assign Resources button (Resource tab) to drag and assign multiple resources at once.






Note



Over-allocation indicator: A red person icon appears in the Indicators column when a resource is assigned more than their Max. Units. Fix with: Resource tab → Level Resources or manually adjust assignments.




9.4.9 Step 9 — Set the Baseline
Before any work begins, freeze the plan:
Project tab → Set Baseline → Set Baseline
This saves the current schedule as Baseline 0. You can compare actual progress against this later. MS Project allows up to 11 baselines (Baseline 0–10).






Important



Set the baseline only when the plan is approved. Once work begins, do not reset the baseline unless formally approved through change control.




9.4.10 Step 10 — Track Progress
As work proceeds, update the schedule:

Mark % complete: Click a task → Task tab → Mark on Track (sets 100% on track) or type % in the % Complete column
Enter actual dates: Double-click task → Advanced tab → enter Actual Start / Actual Finish
Update remaining duration: In the Tracking Gantt, right-click a task → Update Task → enter remaining work

To see schedule variance: View → Tracking Gantt — the black baseline bar appears below the blue (current) bar.

text:
9.8 Common Mistakes to Avoid






Warning⚠️ Top 10 MS Project Mistakes




Starting without a WBS — tasks entered randomly, no structure, impossible to track
All tasks manually scheduled — MS Project cannot recalculate; schedule is just a static table
No dependencies set — tasks float freely; critical path cannot be calculated
Assigning resources before entering all tasks — resource data becomes inconsistent
Never setting a baseline — no way to compare actual vs. planned
Ignoring over-allocation warnings — red resource icons are serious; they mean your plan is unrealistic
Updating % complete without entering actual dates — creates misleading tracking data
Not using a custom calendar — default calendar is Mon–Fri, which is wrong for regional projects
Using MS Project as a spreadsheet — typing static dates instead of letting the scheduling engine calculate them
One file for all versions — always version your file; never overwrite the baseline file

9.9 Exercises






Caution✏️ Exercise 6.1 — Pre-Project Checklist



Before building a schedule in MS Project, a project manager must collect specific information. For the following project scenario, complete all six preparation documents:
Scenario: Your company has won a contract to design and install a solar power system (50 kW) on the roof of a hospital in Ramallah. The project runs for 12 weeks starting 1 March 2026, budget ₪ 280,000.

Write a one-page Project Charter with: objectives, scope, out-of-scope items, key milestones, sponsor, PM, and approved budget
Create a WBS with at least 3 levels (minimum 20 work packages)
Develop an Activity List with durations and dependencies for all Level-3 WBS items
Create a Resource Register for at least 6 resources (mix of people, equipment, material)
List the project calendar exceptions (holidays) for the project period
Identify 3 fixed-date constraints and explain how you would model each in MS Project









Caution✏️ Exercise 6.2 — Build the Schedule in MS Project



Using the preparation documents from Exercise 6.1 (or the template provided by your instructor):

Create a new MS Project file with a custom calendar (Sunday–Thursday, 08:00–17:00)
Enter all tasks with correct WBS indentation (summary tasks and sub-tasks)
Set all tasks to Auto Scheduled mode
Enter durations and predecessor dependencies
Enter all resources in the Resource Sheet (at least 6 resources with correct types and rates)
Assign resources to all tasks
Identify the critical path (Format → Critical Tasks). List all critical tasks and the total project duration
Check for resource over-allocation and resolve at least one conflict using resource levelling
Set the baseline (Project → Set Baseline → Baseline 0)
Export the Gantt Chart as a PDF and the resource cost summary as an Excel file









Caution✏️ Exercise 6.3 — Progress Tracking



Using the schedule you built in Exercise 6.2, simulate 4 weeks of execution:
Week 1 actual data: - All initiation tasks completed on time (100%) - Site survey started 2 days late (actual start = Day 3)
Week 2 actual data: - Site survey completed (3 days instead of planned 5 days — ahead of schedule) - Procurement task started as planned
Week 3 actual data: - Procurement delayed: expected to take 14 days instead of 10 (vendor delayed delivery)
Week 4 actual data: - Procurement still in progress (60% complete) - IP & VLAN Design completed on time

Enter all actual data using the Update Tasks feature and % Complete column
View the Tracking Gantt — which tasks show schedule variance?
Calculate SPI and CPI using the Earned Value report
Identify which activity is now on the critical path due to the procurement delay
Propose a recovery plan: what can be done to bring the project back on track?









Caution✏️ Exercise 6.4 — Reports and Communication



Using your completed MS Project file:

Generate the Project Overview Dashboard report — export as PDF
Generate the Slipping Tasks report — identify all tasks currently behind baseline
Generate the Resource Overview report — identify the most over-allocated resource
Generate the Earned Value report — extract PV, EV, AC, CPI, SPI values for Week 4
Create a custom one-page stakeholder report using the Report Designer (Report tab → New Report → Table) that shows: Task name, Baseline Start, Actual Start, Baseline Finish, % Complete, Cost Variance
Export the task list (File → Save As → Excel Workbook) and format it as a progress table suitable for a weekly status meeting

title: 10  Risk Management & Project Audit
text:
10.1 What is Risk?






Note📖 PMI Definition of Risk




“An uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more project objectives such as scope, schedule, cost, or quality.” — PMBOK® Guide, 7th Edition

Key Insight: Risk ≠ Problem. A risk is a possibility, not a certainty. When a risk occurs, it becomes an issue that must be managed.







flowchart LR
    U["🔮 UNCERTAINTY<br/><br/>We don't know<br/>if this will happen"]
    R["⚠️ RISK<br/><br/>Identified uncertainty<br/>with assessed<br/>probability and impact"]
    T["🎯 TRIGGER<br/><br/>Early warning sign<br/>that risk is<br/>becoming more likely"]
    I["🔥 ISSUE<br/><br/>Risk has occurred —<br/>now must be<br/>actively managed"]
    C["💥 CONSEQUENCE<br/><br/>Schedule delay,<br/>cost overrun,<br/>quality failure"]

    U --> R --> T --> I --> C

10.1.1 Threats vs. Opportunities
Risk can be negative (threats) or positive (opportunities):









Threats
Opportunities




Definition

title: 10  Risk Management & Project Audit
text:
10.2 Risk Identification
Risk identification is an ongoing, collaborative process — not a one-time event at project start.

10.2.1 Risk Identification Techniques

BrainstormingRisk ChecklistsFMEA / HAZIDSWOT AnalysisAssumption and Constraint Analysis


Free-form group ideation in a risk workshop
Process: 1. Assemble cross-functional team (PM, engineers, client rep, external specialist) 2. Use structured prompts: “What could go wrong with…?” 3. Capture all ideas without judgment 4. Categorise and de-duplicate 5. Assess each identified risk
Tips: - Use an experienced facilitator, not the PM (who might inhibit responses) - Time-box: 30-60 minutes per major project phase - Anonymous input methods (sticky notes, digital tools) encourage candid responses


Use historical risk lists from similar projects
Industry-specific checklists exist for: - Civil/structural engineering - Process plant design - IT systems implementation - Environmental projects - Offshore/subsea projects
Checklists ensure common risks are not overlooked but must be supplemented with project-specific risks.


Failure Mode and Effects Analysis / Hazard Identification
Used in engineering and safety-critical industries:

For each component/process, ask: “How can this FAIL?”
For each failure mode: “What is the EFFECT of this failure?”
Assign: Severity, Occurrence probability, Detectability
Calculate Risk Priority Number (RPN): \[RPN = Severity \times Occurrence \times Detectability\]
Focus on highest RPN items



Structured analysis of project context

Negative (address)

Strengths
Weaknesses


External

Threats



Useful for early risk identification and strategic risk assessment. Connect SWOT factors to specific risk scenarios.


Challenge every assumption in the project plan
For each assumption: “What happens if this assumption is WRONG?”
Examples: - “We assumed excavation would encounter class 3 material — what if it’s class 5?” - “We assumed the supplier could deliver in 8 weeks — what if it takes 14?” - “We assumed EPA approval within 6 months — what if it takes 12?”

title: 10  Risk Management & Project Audit
section: Case Study — Mecca Crane Collapse 2015: The Cost of Ignored Risk
text:
Case Study — Mecca Crane Collapse 2015: The Cost of Ignored Risk






Important🏭 Case Study: Masjid al-Haram Crane Collapse — Risk Management Under Deadline Pressure



Background:
On 11 September 2015 — just 11 days before Hajj was due to begin — a Liebherr LR 11350 crane collapsed at the Masjid al-Haram (Grand Mosque of Mecca) construction site during a storm. The crane fell into the mosque’s northern courtyard, directly onto pilgrims performing prayers. The collapse killed 111 people and injured 394 others.
Saudi Binladin Group (SBG), one of the world’s largest construction contractors and the Kingdom’s most prestigious builder, was managing the largest ongoing expansion of Islam’s holiest site.
Risk Management Failures:








Risk Factor
What Should Have Happened
What Actually Happened




Crane securing protocol
Cranes must be secured in travel (free-slew) mode before storms; standards require de-rigging when wind exceeds 72 km/h
Wind reached 83 km/h; the crane remained rigged and unsecured in travel mode


Meteorological monitoring
48-hour advance weather monitoring with automatic crane protocols triggered at defined wind thresholds
A weather alert was issued but not formally communicated to crane operators


Public exclusion zones
Live construction adjacent to an occupied worship space — an extraordinary risk context requiring enhanced protocols
No enhanced exclusion zone protocol existed for public prayer areas below active cranes during extreme weather


Equipment condition
All cranes subject to regular third-party certification
Investigation indicated the crane’s luffing jib pin was in a degraded condition — a known maintenance concern


Risk culture
Supervisors must have authority to halt work for any safety concern
The 11-day countdown to Hajj created “normalisation of deviance” — routine shortcuts had accumulated over weeks without incident



The Normalisation of Deviance:
SBG had worked under intense Hajj-season deadline pressure for decades without a major fatal incident. Shortcuts that deviated from formal safety protocols had become routine because “nothing bad had happened before.” The 2015 collapse demonstrates that statistical tolerance of risk does not reduce the underlying probability of catastrophe — it merely delays it.
Financial and Operational Consequences: - Criminal investigation of SBG management; 13 individuals charged - Following the crane collapse and a separate Mina pilgrimage stampede (24 September 2015), SBG was suspended from all Saudi government contracts by end of 2015 - SBG had revenues exceeding $5 billion/year — the suspension was an existential business event - Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 subsequently restructured the Haramain and Haram construction contracting model entirely
Engineering and PM Lessons: 1. Deadline pressure is the greatest enemy of risk management — the closer the deadline, the more vigilantly risk protocols must be enforced, not relaxed 2. Known equipment deficiencies must be formally entered into the risk register — “we’ll fix it next month” is not a risk response 3. Public safety in and around construction exclusion zones is non-negotiable — it cannot be traded against schedule 4. Risk culture is built over years and destroyed in days — senior project leadership must model expected safety behaviour at peak pressure moments, not only in routine periods 5. “We have always done it this way without incident” is cognitive bias (normalisation of deviance), not a risk assessment
Discussion Questions: 1. Which of the six risk response strategies should SBG have applied to the crane stability risk during a known storm event at an occupied site? 2. What specific trigger events and thresholds should have been included in the risk register to prevent this incident? 3. How does schedule pressure influence risk decision-making on construction projects in the Arab world?
Sources: Al-Harthi and Al-Ghamdi (2016); MEED Projects (2016)

title: 10  Risk Management & Project Audit
text:
10.7 Project Audit
A project audit is a formal, independent assessment of a project conducted at a scheduled point during execution — not just at the end. The goal is to evaluate whether the project is performing as planned, identify corrective actions, and inform a formal go / no-go / restructure decision.






Note📖 Definition — Project Audit



A project audit is a structured, documented review of a project’s performance, processes, and compliance against its approved plan, governance requirements, and applicable standards. It is conducted by an independent reviewer or audit team — not the project team itself.

“The audit examines the reasons for success or failure and, more importantly, extracts lessons that can be applied to improve the management of future projects.” — Meredith & Mantel, Project Management: A Managerial Approach





10.7.1 Types of Project Audit

Types of project audit







Audit Type
Trigger
Focus




In-process Audit
Scheduled (e.g., end of each phase)
Is the project on track? Will it meet objectives?


Pre-completion Audit
Near project end
Are all deliverables complete? Is handover ready?


Termination Audit
When cancellation is being considered
Should the project continue, restructure, or terminate?


Post-project Audit
6–12 months after close
Did the project deliver the expected benefits?






10.7.2 The Audit Process

10.7.3 What the Audit Examines
A comprehensive project audit reviews six key dimensions:

Scope & DeliverablesSchedule PerformanceCost PerformanceRisk & IssuesQuality & ComplianceTeam & Stakeholders

Is there uncontrolled scope growth (scope creep)?

11.1.2 Estimation Techniques

Analogous (Top-Down)ParametricBottom-UpThree-Point (PERT)


Based on historical data from similar projects
\[Cost_{new} = Cost_{historical} \times Adjustment\ Factor\]
When to use: Early project stages; limited detail available
Cost Capacity Factor (Six-Tenths Rule): \[Cost_B = Cost_A \times \left(\frac{Capacity_B}{Capacity_A}\right)^{0.6}\]
Example: “Our last desalination plant (50 ML/day) cost $85M. This one is 65 ML/day:
$85M × (65/50)^{0.6} = $85M × 1.21 ≈ $103M”
Accuracy: ±25% to ±50%


Mathematical models based on units of measure
Examples: - Civil works: $450/m² × 3,500 m² = $1,575,000 - Earthworks: $28/m³ × 15,000 m³ = $420,000 - Electrical: $650/circuit × 180 circuits = $117,000
Accuracy: ±10% to ±25%


Estimate each work package individually, then sum
Most accurate; most time-consuming.
For each activity: 1. Materials: Quantity × Unit rate 2. Labour: Hours × Hourly rate 3. Equipment: Hours/days × Hire rate 4. Overheads: (L + M + E) × OH% 5. Profit/margin (for contractors)
Accuracy: ±5% to ±15%


Optimistic, Most Likely, Pessimistic applied to cost
\[CE = \frac{O + 4M + P}{6}\]
Used to build cost contingency from risk analysis.

Cost control involves monitoring, forecasting, and taking corrective action:

    R --> |"No"| CA["⚠️ Corrective Action<br/>Identify root cause<br/>Develop & approve plan"]
    CA --> U["📋 UPDATE<br/>Revised estimate<br/>Change request & report"]

    CO --> M

    style M fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6

    style CA fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444
    style CO fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e


 Cost control cycle 




11.7.1 Cost Control Techniques

EVM TrendingCost ForecastingChange ControlRecovery Strategies


Monitor CPI and SPI trends weekly: - Is CPI improving or deteriorating? - Historical research shows: CPI rarely improves by more than 10% from its value at 20% project completion - Early warning: CPI < 0.9 at 20% completion = high overrun risk


Review EAC regularly and communicate honestly: - EAC = BAC/CPI — if current cost performance continues (most common) - EAC = AC + (BAC−EV) — if remaining work will be done at original budget - EAC = AC + ETC — if an independent re-estimate of remaining work is done
Compare all three forecasts monthly — divergence signals problems.


All cost changes must go through formal change control: 1. Identify cost trending beyond threshold (typically ±5%) 2. Issue early warning notice to client 3. Raise formal change request 4. Get written approval before spending additional funds


When the project is over budget: 1. Value Engineering — achieve same outcome at lower cost 2. Scope reduction — formally remove lower-priority deliverables 3. Productivity improvement — identify and remove bottlenecks 4. Procurement re-negotiation — re-tender over-budget packages 5. Request Management Reserve — request release from sponsor

NoteMicrosoft Project: Applying Chapter 7 Concepts



With resources and rates assigned in your project file, MS Project can calculate and track costs automatically:
Tasks to complete in MS Project:

Verify resource rates are entered correctly in the Resource Sheet (Std. Rate, Ovt. Rate, Cost/Use, Accrue At = Prorated for most resources)
Add fixed costs: In Gantt Chart view, right-click a column header → Insert Column → Fixed Cost. Enter any fixed procurement or subcontract costs directly against the relevant task
View the Cost table: View → Table → Cost. This shows Baseline Cost, Actual Cost, Remaining Cost, and Cost Variance for every task
Check the project total cost: Project tab → Project Information → Statistics button. Verify the total cost matches your bottom-up estimate
Set the cost baseline (if not already done): Project → Set Baseline → this freezes Baseline Cost values
Enter progress for 3–4 weeks of your project (% Complete per task using actual data or the exercise data from Chapter 6 Exercise 6.3)
Generate the Earned Value report: Report tab → Costs → Earned Value Report. Read off:

PV (Planned Value / BCWS) — shown as “Baseline Cost” at the status date
EV (Earned Value / BCWP) — shown as “Earned Value”
AC (Actual Cost / ACWP) — shown as “Actual Cost”
CPI and SPI — calculated automatically
EAC (Estimate at Completion) — MS Project uses EAC = BAC / CPI by default

Set the Status Date: Project tab → Project Information → Status Date. MS Project uses this date when calculating EV metrics — set it to the end of your last reported week
View the Tracking Gantt and identify tasks where Cost Variance (CV) is negative (over budget). What corrective actions would you recommend?

title: 12  Quality Management
section: 12.1 What is Quality in Engineering Projects?
text:
12.1 What is Quality in Engineering Projects?






Note📖 Two Dimensions of Quality



Quality of Design (Fitness for Purpose):
Does the delivered product meet the intended purpose? Did we deliver what the client NEEDED?
Quality of Conformance (Conformance to Specifications):
Was the product built exactly to the approved specifications, drawings, and standards?
Example: A bridge designed for 40-tonne trucks but only used by cars is HIGH quality of conformance (built as designed) but potentially POOR quality of design (over-engineered = waste). A bridge designed for 100-tonne loads but built with B-grade steel is HIGH quality of design but POOR quality of conformance.



12.1.1 Grade vs. Quality









High Grade
Low Grade




High Quality
Premium product built to spec
Budget product built to spec


Low Quality
Premium product with defects
Budget product with defects



Grade is the level of performance requirements; Quality is whether those requirements are met.

Note📖 QA vs. QC — The Critical Distinction



Quality Assurance (QA): Focuses on processes — “Are we doing the right things the right way?” - Proactive and process-oriented - Performed DURING the project - Examples: Process audits, design reviews, peer checks, construction supervision
Quality Control (QC): Focuses on outputs — “Does the product meet requirements?” - Reactive and product-oriented - Applied to completed work - Examples: Material testing, dimensional surveys, pressure testing, functional testing

A Quality Management Plan (QMP) defines how quality will be managed throughout the project:

title: 12  Quality Management
text:
12.7 Cost of Quality
The Cost of Quality (CoQ) model recognises that ALL quality activities have a cost — and that investing in prevention is far cheaper than paying for failures:

Prevention CostsAppraisal CostsInternal Failure CostsExternal Failure Costs


Costs to prevent defects (proactive): - Quality planning and QMP development - Staff training and competency assessment - Design reviews and peer checks - Process standardisation and procedure writing - Supplier qualification programmes - Quality audits
Cost: Low-medium; Returns: Very high


Costs to detect defects (inspection): - Material testing (concrete tests, weld inspections) - Site inspections and surveys - Software testing - Third-party audits and certifications - Equipment calibration
Cost: Medium; Returns: Medium-high


Defects found BEFORE delivery: - Rework (fixing defects before client sees them) - Scrap (material wasted due to errors) - Redesign required - Re-testing after rework
Cost: High; Avoided by prevention and appraisal


Defects found AFTER delivery: - Warranty claims and rectification - Legal liability - Lost future business - Regulatory fines - Brand damage - Property damage or personal injury
Cost: Extremely high; Avoided by good QA/QC









Warning⚠️ The 1-10-100 Rule of Quality



The cost of fixing a defect multiplies with how late it is discovered:

Cost to prevent (design stage): $1
Cost to detect and fix (during construction): $10
Cost to fix after handover (warranty claim): $100

This is why front-end investment in quality planning and design reviews has the highest ROI in engineering projects.

title: 12  Quality Management
section: Case Study — Jeddah Floods 2009: The Hidden Cost of Quality Failure
text:
Case Study — Jeddah Floods 2009: The Hidden Cost of Quality Failure






Important🏭 Case Study: Jeddah Flooding — When Quality Assurance Is the First Budget Cut



Background:
On 25 November 2009, a single rainstorm struck Jeddah, Saudi Arabia — 90 mm of rain in 3 hours, equivalent to the city’s entire annual average rainfall in one event. The results were catastrophic: 161 officially confirmed deaths (independent estimates suggest over 500), thousands of vehicles swept away, and entire residential districts submerged under metres of water. The Saudi government subsequently spent over SAR 35 billion (~$9 billion) in disaster response and infrastructure reconstruction.
The engineering tragedy was not the rainfall — extreme flash floods are a known geological risk in the Hejaz region. The tragedy was the absence of drainage infrastructure that should have been built and inspected years earlier.
What the Post-Disaster Investigation Found:
A Saudi Control and Investigation Board inquiry revealed systematic quality management failure across decades of city infrastructure development:








Infrastructure Element
Required
Actually Built




Primary storm drainage network
500 km specified in master plan
~200 km built; much of it blocked by sediment and illegal connections


Retention ponds
15 major retention basins required
3 completed; 8 plot allocations reassigned to housing developers


Road drainage channels
Minimum 600 mm kerb drainage on all major roads
Most roads had 200–300 mm drainage; many had none


Construction inspections
All drainage works inspected before roadway overlay
Independent estimates: 60%+ of roads paved without drainage inspection sign-off



Quality Management Failures:
1. Paper-Based QA Without Field Verification:
Contractors routinely submitted quality inspection certificates for works that had not been completed to specification. No independent inspector challenged the certificates. The “quality assurance system” was form completion — not field verification.
2. Cost of Quality Inversion:
Prevention cost (installing the missing drainage correctly): estimated at SAR 1.3 billion.
Failure cost paid (disaster response, reconstruction, compensation): SAR 35+ billion.
This is a 27:1 ratio — a textbook demonstration of how eliminating quality investment creates catastrophic failure costs.
3. Conflict of Interest in QA Oversight:
The municipal authority, urban development office, and construction contractors were linked through business and family relationships — structural compromises to QA independence that allowed systemic non-conformance to persist undetected.
4. Accumulation of “Acceptable” Non-Conformances:
Individual drainage shortfalls in each development project were classified as “non-material NCRs” and signed off. Over 20 years of rapid city growth, thousands of individually approved NCRs accumulated into a completely broken citywide drainage system.
The True Cost of Quality — Jeddah 2009:








Cost Category
Amount
Notes




Emergency response
SAR 4.8 billion
Immediate


Road and drainage reconstruction
SAR 6.2 billion
Multi-year programme


Compensation to bereaved families
SAR 0.3 billion



Lost business and private property
SAR 12+ billion
Estimated


Prevention cost if QA had functioned
SAR 1.3 billion
Full drainage system cost



Quality Lessons: 1. QA independence is not a luxury — when the inspector and contractor share financial interests, there is no quality assurance 2. The cost of preventing quality failure is always a fraction of the failure cost — quality is never the line to cut in a budget overrun 3. Individual NCRs accumulate systemic risk — no single non-conformance appears catastrophic in isolation; the pattern of non-conformances is 4. Paper-based QA systems are not quality systems — quality assurance requires field verification and independent sign-off, not form completion 5. Quality culture requires consequences — if contractors face no accountability for non-conformance, non-conformance will be universal
Discussion Questions: 1. Which quality management process (Planning, QA, or QC) failed most catastrophically in this case? 2. Design a quality audit programme that would have detected the drainage infrastructure failures before they became a crisis 3. How does this case illustrate the relationship between procurement governance, stakeholder independence, and quality outcomes in rapidly developing Arab cities?
Sources: Saudi Geological Survey (2010); Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development (2010)

title: 13  Agile Project Management & Scrum
text:
13.1 The Agile Mindset
Traditional (Waterfall) project management assumes that requirements can be fully defined at the start and that the best approach is to plan completely before executing.
Agile was born from the recognition that many projects — especially in software, R&D, and innovative engineering — operate in environments where:

Requirements evolve and change
The problem is not fully understood at the start
Frequent feedback from users is more valuable than following a fixed plan
Early delivery of partial value is better than waiting for complete delivery







Note📖 The Agile Manifesto (2001)



The Agile Manifesto (Beck et al. 2001) states four core values:



We value…
…over




Individuals and interactions
Processes and tools


Working software
Comprehensive documentation


Customer collaboration
Contract negotiation


Responding to change
Following a plan




“That is, while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more.”

Note: Agile does NOT say “no documentation” or “no planning” — it says the items on the LEFT are prioritised when they conflict with the items on the RIGHT.

13.2 The Scrum Framework
Scrum is the most widely used Agile framework. It organises work into short, time-boxed iterations called Sprints:

 The Scrum Framework — complete overview 




13.2.1 The Three Scrum Roles

Product OwnerScrum MasterDevelopment Team


Maximises value of the product/project
Responsibilities: - Maintains and prioritises the Product Backlog - Ensures the team understands what needs to be built AND why - Accepts or rejects sprint output (is it “done”?) - Represents the voice of the customer/user/stakeholder - Has authority to make product decisions
In Engineering Context:
The Product Owner might be the client’s lead engineer, the project sponsor’s representative, or a senior PM who can make real-time scope decisions.


Guardian of the Scrum process
Responsibilities: - Facilitates all Scrum ceremonies (planning, daily scrum, review, retrospective) - Removes impediments (blockers that prevent the team from working) - Coaches the team on Scrum practices - Shields the team from external interruptions during sprints - NOT a traditional PM — does not assign tasks or manage people
Important: The Scrum Master serves the team, not the other way around.


Self-organising, cross-functional group that builds the product
Characteristics: - Self-organising: Team decides HOW to do the work; no sub-teams - Cross-functional: All skills needed to complete a sprint are within the team - Accountable: Team owns delivery of the sprint goal, not individuals - Size: Typically 3-9 people (smaller = more agile; larger = more communication overhead)
In Engineering Context:
Might include mechanical engineers, software developers, test engineers, and documentation specialists — all working together within the sprint rather than in separate sequential phases.

The team selects items it can complete within the sprint based on: - Velocity (average story points completed per sprint, from historical data) - Sprint Goal (the objective of this specific sprint) - Capacity (team availability, accounting for leave, meetings, etc.)
A Sprint Backlog item should be completable within one sprint. If too large, it is decomposed into smaller tasks.

Definition of Done (DoD): A shared understanding of what “completed” means. For each story/feature: - Code written and reviewed (for software) - Tests written and passing - Documentation updated - Stakeholder accepted
For Engineering: DoD might include design calculations checked, drawings peer-reviewed, and client acceptance received.

title: 13  Agile Project Management & Scrum
section: Case Study — Agile in the Arab World: Amman Smart Traffic Management
text:
Case Study — Agile in the Arab World: Amman Smart Traffic Management






Important🏭 Case Study: Amman Adaptive Traffic Control — Jordan’s First Agile Public Infrastructure Delivery



Background:
Greater Amman Municipality (GAM) contracted a Jordanian-European consortium in 2018 to deliver an Adaptive Traffic Control System (ATCS) across 350 signalised intersections in central Amman. The Ministry of Public Works had previously attempted a similar system in 2012 using a traditional waterfall approach — that $6.2 million contract was cancelled after 18 months with zero intersections operational.
This time, GAM insisted on an Agile delivery framework — a first for Jordan’s public sector infrastructure.
The Challenge:
An ATCS is never “finished” in the traditional sense. Requirements were incompletely understood at project start, Amman’s road network was evolving (3 new road tunnels under simultaneous construction), traffic data was sparse, and 15 stakeholder departments (traffic police, urban planning, emergency services, bus operators, Civil Defence) had conflicting priorities.
Agile Adoption:
1. Scrum for Software and Algorithm Development: - 2-week sprints for traffic algorithm development, CCTV integration, and the control dashboard - Product backlog maintained by a GAM Traffic Engineer acting as Product Owner — a government employee, not a consultant - Daily standups conducted in Arabic; sprint reviews included representatives from Amman Traffic Police - Definition of “Done” required each intersection to pass a 48-hour silent monitoring trial before being counted complete
2. Traditional Engineering for Physical Infrastructure: - Cabinet installation, fibre cable laying, and inductive detector loops retained standard engineering approval workflows - Physical works were batched into “packages” aligned with each sprint’s software scope — a genuine Hybrid delivery model
3. Sprint Cadence: - Sprints 1–4: Core system architecture, 10-intersection pilot (Downtown Amman), baseline traffic data collection - Sprints 5–9: Adaptive algorithm v1.0 deployed across 80 intersections; emergency vehicle pre-emption logic - Sprints 10–16: Corridor coordination (5 major arterials linking central districts); public information displays; GAM staff training - Sprints 17+: Expansion programme, remote monitoring portal, Ministry of Interior integration
Results: - First 10 intersections operational within 6 weeks of contract start (previously 18 months with zero result under waterfall) - 350 intersections fully integrated within 18 months, on schedule and within 3% of budget - Average peak-hour journey time on the Al-Medina Street corridor reduced by 22% in Year 1 - Client satisfaction: 8.7/10; GAM extended the contract for 400 additional intersections before the original scope was complete - The Arabic-language system interface and Arabic training materials were embedded from Sprint 1 — not added as an afterthought
Key Agile Lessons for Arab Engineers: 1. Deliver something working as early as possible — GAM saw 10 live intersections in Week 6; this rebuilt institutional trust that the 2012 failure had destroyed 2. Agile works in Arabic — the Scrum framework adapts to any language or cultural context; the Product Owner role was equally effective in a government setting 3. Hybrid is the norm in infrastructure — physical works followed standard engineering governance; algorithm and software development used Agile 4. Local ownership is critical — embedding a GAM engineer as Product Owner (not a consultant) ensured the system matched real operational needs, not theoretical requirements 5. Early failure is cheap — the 10-intersection pilot failed three times before the algorithm was tuned correctly; those failures cost days, not months

title: 14  Project Closure & Lessons Learned
text:
14.1 Why Closure Matters
Many project managers treat closure as an afterthought — a few admin tasks after the “real” work is done. This is a critical mistake. Poor closure leads to:

Knowledge loss: Lessons not captured become repeated mistakes
Contractual exposure: Final payments withheld due to incomplete documentation
Operational failures: Handover packages that leave the operations team unable to maintain the system
Stakeholder dissatisfaction: No formal recognition or celebration of achievement
Regulatory non-compliance: Missing as-built records, certifications, or permits-to-operate







Note📖 What is Project Closure?



PMBOK defines Project Closure as the process of finalising all activities across all Project Management Process Groups to formally complete or close a project, phase, or contract.
Closure activities are typically triggered by: - Normal completion: All deliverables accepted, objectives met - Phase-gate closure: End of a project phase before beginning the next - Premature termination: Project cancelled, merged, or made redundant - Contractual completion: Final payment received, warranty period ended



14.1.1 Types of Closure

14.4.1 Running a Lessons Learned Workshop

PreparationDuring the WorkshopOutput Format


Before the Workshop: 1. Schedule 2-3 hours for a team of up to 12 people 2. Invite all key project contributors (not just the core PM team) 3. Circulate a brief pre-read with timeline, key milestones, and objectives vs. actuals 4. Prepare a structured template for capturing inputs 5. Appoint an objective facilitator (ideally not the PM, to prevent defensiveness)
Ground Rules: - This is a “blameless” session — we focus on systems and processes, not people - Be specific: give examples and data - Every insight is valuable — nothing is too small - Action items must have owners and dates


Structure the session using the following prompts:

section: 14.6 The Human Side of Closure — Tuckman “Adjourning”
text:
14.6 The Human Side of Closure — Tuckman “Adjourning”
Tuckman’s model of team development (introduced in Chapter 5) includes a final stage often overlooked:





flowchart LR
    T1["Forming<br/>😐 Polite,<br/>uncertain"] --> T2
    T2["Storming<br/>😤 Conflict,<br/>competing"] --> T3
    T3["Norming<br/>🤝 Rules,<br/>cooperation"] --> T4
    T4["Performing<br/>🚀 High output,<br/>confidence"] --> T5
    T5["Adjourning<br/>😢 Disengagement,<br/>reflection<br/>(project closure)"]

    style T5 fill:#4f46e5,color:#fff


 Tuckman’s model — the Adjourning stage 



The Adjourning Stage is characterised by: - Pride and satisfaction — recognition of what the team achieved - Anxiety — uncertainty about what comes next for individuals - Loss — the end of a high-performing team and valued relationships - Reflection — individuals processing the project experience
PM’s Role During Adjourning: 1. Acknowledge and celebrate achievement — project launch event, awards, team dinner 2. Express genuine appreciation for individual contributions (personal, not just generic) 3. Provide career guidance — help team members secure their next opportunity 4. Manage the transition — clear timelines for when people are released 5. Write references and performance reviews promptly 6. Capture team expertise in lessons learned before knowledge disperses

text:
14.7 The Final Project Completion Report
The Project Completion Report is delivered to the sponsor/steering committee and documents the full project story:






Note📖 Project Completion Report Structure



1. Executive Summary
One-page overview of what was delivered, key outcomes vs. objectives, and top 5 lessons learned.
2. Project Overview
Background, objectives, scope, key stakeholders, and delivery strategy.
3. Deliverables Summary
Table of all contracted deliverables — delivered/not delivered; scope variations.
4. Schedule Performance
Planned vs. actual dates for key milestones; causes of delays or early completions.
5. Cost Performance
Final cost vs. approved budget; variance analysis; EVM final metrics.
6. Quality Performance
Key QA/QC metrics — NCR count, inspection result rates, rework costs, defects at completion.
7. Risk Summary
Top risks identified at start, how they materialised (or didn’t), risk management effectiveness.
8. Stakeholder Satisfaction
Survey results, any outstanding concerns, relationship outcomes.
9. Lessons Learned Summary
Top 10 lessons (both positive and negative) to be implemented on future projects.
10. Recommendations
Specific recommendations for the organisation, operations team, and future projects.

title: 14  Project Closure & Lessons Learned
section: Case Study — Doha Metro: Closing the Arab World’s Most Complex New Railway
text:
Case Study — Doha Metro: Closing the Arab World’s Most Complex New Railway






Important🏭 Case Study: Doha Metro — Planned Closure, Delivered On Time



Background:
The Doha Metro (مترو الدوحة) is Qatar’s first urban rail network — 76 km of track, 3 lines, 37 stations, built almost entirely underground in 7 years. Qatar Rail awarded construction contracts in 2013 with a committed Phase 1 opening of May 2019 to support Qatar’s growing sporting calendar leading toward the FIFA World Cup 2022. Phase 1 closure was itself a complex project-within-a-project: opening a live metro in a city that had never had one before.
Planned Opening: May 2019
Actual Opening: May 2019 — on time, a remarkable achievement for a programme of this scale
Phase 1 Budget: Approximately $36 billion (full network, including tunnels and stations)
Closure Challenges:
1. Multi-Contractor Systems Integration:
The Doha Metro involved over 60 major contracts across civil works, MEP systems, rolling stock (CRRC trains), signalling (Thales), communications (Siemens), and station fit-out. No single contractor was responsible end-to-end.
Solution: Qatar Rail appointed a dedicated Systems Integration Manager (SIM) 30 months before opening, with authority to issue binding interface instructions to all contractors regardless of contract. This role resolved 340+ documented interface non-conformances before they could delay the opening.
2. Regulatory Certification — A New Challenge for Qatar:
Qatar had never had a metro. The national rail safety regulatory framework was being developed in parallel with the project — an extraordinary risk that certification could be delayed regardless of construction readiness.
Solution: Qatar Rail engaged European rail safety certification specialists (CERTIFER, France) to prepare the safety case 18 months in advance; a “shadow” regulatory review 12 months before submission identified and resolved 28 regulatory gaps before the formal certification submission.
3. Phased Commissioning (Not a Big-Bang Opening):
Rather than one simultaneous closure event, the handover strategy was incremental: - Tunnel infrastructure accepted: 18 months before opening - Train delivery and depot commissioning: 12 months before opening - Station MEP systems accepted: 6 months before opening - Trial operations (full-readiness, no public): 3 months before opening - Revenue operations Phase 1: May 2019
Each phase had formal acceptance criteria, independent verification, and documented handover packs.
4. Operations Workforce Transition:
At construction peak, the programme employed over 45,000 workers. The closure plan managed the transition to an operations workforce of 2,200: - Operations staff recruited and trained in parallel with commissioning — not after it - 200-day train driver simulator programme before any revenue operation - Formal knowledge transfer: 18 months of shadowing between construction engineers and operations maintenance teams

Takeaway for Engineers:
The Doha Metro’s successful closure was the result of closure planning from day one — not as a phase added at the end. The Systems Integration Manager role, phased handover strategy, parallel operations recruitment, and proactive regulatory engagement were all written into the project execution plan at contract award. The lesson: you close well only if you plan to close well from the beginning.

You are preparing to facilitate a lessons-learned workshop for a 3-year desalination plant project. The project delivered on scope and quality but was 8 months late and 12% over budget. The team of 15 core members will attend.

Caution✏️ Exercise 10.3 — Benefits Realisation Assessment



A new wastewater treatment plant upgrade was justified in the business case with the following benefits: - 40% reduction in energy consumption (baseline: $2.2M/year opex) - 100% compliance with new EPA nitrogen limits (≤10 mg/L total nitrogen) - 30% reduction in odour complaints - Capacity increase from 80 ML/day to 120 ML/day
One year after handover, the following data is available: - Energy costs: $1.6M (vs. $2.2M baseline) - EPA compliance: 94% of samples within limits (6 samples failed over 12 months) - Odour complaints: 22 this year (vs. 35 baseline year) - Peak day flow recorded: 115 ML/day (design capacity 120 ML/day)

Calculate the variance for each benefit against the target
Which benefits were achieved, partially achieved, and not achieved?
For any benefit not fully achieved, what could be the cause and what remediation would you recommend?
Should the project be declared a “success”? Discuss using the triple constraint AND the benefits realisation lens.
